articles.summary: From Moscow to Plesetsk, Ukraine appears to be trying to hit infrastructure that powers Russia’s war from space.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – Russian Aerospace Forces (RAF) chief Aleksandr Chayko barely survived a blast that killed his son-in-law.

Chayko, who turned 55 in the last week of July, was reportedly having a belated birthday party on August 1 at a high-end Italian restaurant in central Moscow.

But the celebration was cut short, as an ‌unidentified woman carrying a homemade bomb tried to enter the restaurant. She was stopped by a security ‌guard, according to Russia. The explosive in her bag detonated, killing at least five people.

The Kremlin did not confirm the casualties, but blamed the attack on the “bloody tentacles” of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s government.

Russia’s space programme in the firing line

Chayko helped lead Russia’s intervention in Syria and commanded Russian forces north of Kyiv in early 2022.

In May, President Vladimir Putin appointed him commander-in-chief of the RAF that controls the military component of Russia’s space programme.

The RAF’s satellites and ground-space facilities have been used for gathering intelligence, navigation, and supporting the coordination of ground troops and drone and missile attacks.

These facilities are located mostly in western Russia, and new Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles are capable of striking them.

“Key factories are few, and they all are within the reach of Ukrainian missiles,” Nikolay Mitrokhin, a researcher with Germany’s University of Bremen, told Al Jazeera.

“These attacks may result – and certainly will – in the problems with all of Russia’s space programme, including specifically civilian and international programmes,” he said.

In late June, Ukrainian drones hit the giant space communications centre in the leafy, tranquil town of Dubna outside Moscow that managed reconnaissance satellites and processed military data.

The strike damaged a 32-metre (105-foot) satellite antenna, hardware modular complexes, central control consoles and technical buildings.

“Our long-range sanctions against Russia for this war once again reached the Dubna space communications centre,” Zelenskyy said on June 30.

Russian authorities said an unspecified building in Dubna was damaged and a six-month-old baby died.

Ukrainian drones also struck three smaller space communication centres in western Russia and annexed Crimea.

“These centres are very expensive, very labour-consuming from the viewpoint of construction,” Anatoly Zak, a United States-based author and one of the foremost experts on the Russian space programme, told Al Jazeera. “It’s very difficult to transfer their functions to another infrastructure” because they manage geostationary satellites “tied” to a certain location.

So far, there have been no signs that the satellites lost orbit or became unmanageable, but “behind the scenes there are for sure serious communication problems”, Zak said.

Ukraine attacks ‘when there’s a fully-fuelled rocket on the launchpad’

On August 23, swarms of Ukrainian drones flew more than 1,800km (1,120 miles) to reach Russia’s northwestern Arkhangelsk region.

Some 40 drones were downed, regional authorities claimed, but at least two reached the area near Plesetsk, Russia’s military cosmodrome, or spaceport, and launchpad for intercontinental ballistic missiles and rockets carrying military satellites.

No harm was done. A day later, Roscosmos, the state-run space corporation, reported the successful launch of a rocket with unnamed “military satellites”.

The timing of the Ukrainian attack – along with two more strikes earlier this year – was calculated to strike a booster rocket that had just been fuelled and lifted for takeoff.

“There have been three attempts to air-raid Plesetsk, and not just air-raid, but air-raid at the moment when there’s a fully-fuelled rocket on the launchpad that is about to start,” Zak said.

The attempts were serious enough to be publicly reported to Putin.

“Our [Ukrainian] ‘friends’ did everything to make this launch not happen,” Dmitry Bakanov, head of the Kremlin-run Roscosmos space agency, told Putin in April.

At least a dozen drones are necessary to damage Plesetsk’s launch table or rocket assembly shop, according to Pavel Luzin, an analyst with the Jamestown Foundation, a think tank in Washington, DC.

The military satellites launched from Plesetsk are part of the Rassvet (Dawn) satellite fleet designed to rival and replace Starlink satellite modems by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company, Moscow claimed.

Sputnik 1, the Earth’s first artificial satellite, was the size of a fitness ball, and had nothing but a radio transmitter and three silver-zinc batteries inside.

The “Sputnik moment” was the US’s realisation, after the Soviet Union launched the first satellite in 1957, that the USSR had taken the lead in space technology and science.

But Sputnik 1 was launched on a modified R-7 – the world’s first intercontinental ballistic missile, designed to carry a hydrogen bomb across continents. The same rocket technology that could deliver a nuclear warhead into the US had been repurposed to put a satellite into orbit.

The R-7 became a prototype of the Soyuz booster rockets, the world’s most launched spaceships that made Soviet and then Russian launches routine and precise, unlike US launches of space shuttles.

“Rain or shine or sleet or snow don’t matter,” Mark Bowman, deputy director of NASA’s human spaceflight programme, told this reporter in 2007 at the Baikonur spaceport, the world’s oldest in southern Kazakhstan that Russia leases.

The only place where the Soyuz rockets are produced is the Progress Rocket and Space Centre in the Volga River city of Samara – and Ukrainian missiles struck it on August 15. The attack ignited a fire and slightly damaged one of the facilities.

“So far, we see that the damage in Samara wasn’t critical,” Luzin said.

If it becomes critical, Russia would be unable to manufacture the Soyuz rockets, but the existing stash of rockets would still last a year, he said.

Communist Moscow never advertised the military component of its space programme, emphasising its “peaceful exploration of space”.

The USSR was first to send a dog, a man and a woman into space, and to launch the world’s first space station. In 1988, its Buran space shuttle became the first to complete an unmanned orbital flight and land automatically.

Its unmanned probes soft-landed on Venus and Mars and took the first photos of the moon’s dark side.

Some key figures of the Soviet space programmes were born in what is now Ukraine, and a string of crucial design bureaus and manufacturing facilities kept working there after the 1991 Soviet collapse.

Following Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and the subsequent breakdown in Russian-Ukrainian relations, Ukrainian aerospace facilities severed their longstanding ties with Moscow, disrupting decades-old supplies of booster rockets, guidance systems, electronics and other components.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine also deepened the international isolation of its civilian space programme, with Western governments and space agencies suspending or abandoning several planned missions and partnerships.

After the war began in 2022, the European Space Agency terminated its cooperation with Roscosmos on ExoMars, removing the Russian-built Kazachok landing platform from the mission designed to search for signs of past life on Mars.

The same year, Berlin switched off its X-ray telescope on Spektr-RG, a Russia-German space observatory that maps clusters of galaxies and surveys the universe for black holes.

For the sake of seizing insignificant areas in eastern Ukraine, “Putin will waste the Russian space programme the way he wasted the rest of the Soviet legacy”, analyst Mitrokhin believes.

Yet Russia has not been completely cut off from international space cooperation.

Despite the collapse of some partnerships, NASA and Roscosmos have continued to work together on board the International Space Station, while Moscow has turned to China and other non-Western partners for new projects.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy jury remains deadlocked on 6th day of deliberations as mistrial looms
articles.summary: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial have one last chance to reach a verdict before Judge William Sullivan can declare a mistrial in a case that has captivated the nation for the last six weeks.
articles.body: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial have one last chance to reach a verdict before Judge William Sullivan can declare a mistrial in a case that has captivated the nation for the last six weeks. After returning from lunch Wednesday at 2 p.m., the jury handed Sullivan its second deadlock notice, alerting the court that after nearly five days of deliberations, the nine women and three men could not reach a unanimous decision on Clancy’s fate. That note followed the first one, which came Tuesday morning. Sullivan can only send the jury back to deliberate twice before he is able to declare a mistrial, unless the jury consents to more days of deliberations. After the second deadlock note, he gave jurors Tuey-Rodriguez instructions, which essentially asks them to give deliberations one last chance and tells them that it’s “desirable” they reach a verdict. If they return with a third deadlock note Thursday, Sullivan will likely declare a mistrial. But defense attorney Kevin Reddington has insisted that he is ready to go for a second trial, telling reporters outside the courthouse in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Thursday morning that he would be ready as early as next week. Prosecutors have not indicated whether they, too, will be ready for a new trial that soon, or whether they want to retry the case at all. The jury must decide whether Clancy is criminally responsible in the killing of her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — on Jan. 24, 2023, before she threw herself out of her bedroom window in a suicide attempt that left her paralyzed and in a wheelchair. Reddington has argued that Clancy was in the throes of postpartum psychosis at the time the children were killed, and she was compelled to act on auditory hallucinations commanding her to carry out the killings. Prosecutors, however, insist that Clancy was not in a state of psychosis when she strangled the children with exercise bands, and argued that she planned the killings ahead of time, sending her then-husband out for errands when she wanted to carry out the attacks. While the prosecution has sought a first-degree murder conviction, which would carry a life sentence, the jury can also convict Clancy of lesser charges — second-degree murder or manslaughter — or deem her not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility.

articles.title: In Nepal, mourners hold symbolic cremation for missing loved ones
articles.summary: The wall of ice, water and rock that tore through Nepal last week has claimed more than 1,200 lives and left more than 4,000 missing, depriving many grieving families of a basic rite: funerals.
articles.body: The wall of ice, water and rock that tore through Nepal last week has claimed more than 1,200 lives and left more than 4,000 missing, depriving many grieving families of a basic rite: funerals. The scale of the disaster has proved challenging for authorities, with morgues overwhelmed by a large number of unidentified remains. In many cases, bodies have been washed far downstream and rendered unrecognizable, while others still missing are feared to have been buried in the torrent of thick mud. As hopes fade that survivors will be found, a week on from the disaster, family members without the remains of their loved ones have begun to hold symbolic cremations. The ceremonies provide an outlet for the grief and uncertainty that have gripped so many in Nepal, and ensure that a key religious rite is afforded to the dead. At Kathmandu’s Pashupatinath Temple, the most revered Hindu temple in Nepal, mourners gathered Wednesday to mark the loss of missing loved ones. On the banks of the holy Bagmati River, they burned effigies made of kusa grass, also called darbha, a plant used in Hindu rituals, on miniature funeral pyres. The small stick figures, wrapped in orange cloth, were rubbed in paste and covered in garlands of orange flowers. Some relatives, overwhelmed by the moment, collapsed into the arms of their loved ones as they took part in the ceremony. The temple, with its pagoda-style roof, has been around for centuries and is considered one of the most important Hindu pilgrimage sites in Asia. Nepali service members, dressed in military fatigues and holding rifles, provided military honors as they stood along the steps that lead down from the temple to the river. Cremation is an important part of Hindu funeral tradition, and there has been frustration among some relatives of the missing that mass burials, which authorities say is necessary in order to prevent the spread of disease, are being carried out without the consent of the families. Local officials say that they’ve taken DNA samples and photos of corpses to aid later identification. Bodies identified after a mass burial could be exhumed and handed over to the families, officials say.

articles.title: Somalia repels armed assault on Baidoa amid regional political tensions
articles.summary: Explosions and gunfire rock Baidoa as armed groups strike during South West State’s political tensions.
articles.body:
Somalia’s military says it has repelled an attack by two armed groups in Baidoa, the largest city in Somalia’s South West State.

In a statement posted on X, Somalia’s Defence Ministry said “militias” loyal to ousted Governor Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen launched the attack early on Thursday morning.

“The attack began with explosions intended to terrorise civilians, but the army said it responded bravely and inflicted a heavy defeat on the attackers,” the ministry said in a statement.

Several states in the deeply fragmented country are opposed to control by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, who also faces a long-running rebellion by the armed group al-Shabab, which controls vast swathes of central Somalia.

In March, the government sent in troops to oust Laftagareen.

He launched a failed attempt to retake the state in May, and in August his forces fought federal forces for control of Baidoa.

The fighting on Thursday lasted for several hours. Witnesses told AFP that gunfire and explosions could be heard in different parts of the town, forcing residents to remain indoors.

A spokesperson for the pro-Laftagareen forces told AFP that they had captured parts of the city and that fighting was ongoing.

However, several residents told AFP that Baidoa was calm after six hours of battles.

The Defence Ministry said it was investigating the number of fighters killed during the attack and would release details “once the assessment has been completed”.

The ministry also accused the armed groups of operating alongside “al-Shabab terrorists”.

Laftagareen was among the opponents of President Mohamud’s attempts to move Somalia towards democratic elections, replacing a system based around clan elders.

articles.title: What to Know About the Up&Up Baby Wipes Recall at Target
articles.summary: Target has recalled Up&Up Baby Wipes for having life-threatening bacterial contaminants — I spoke to a pediatric infectious disease specialist to find out how this could effect you and your family.
articles.body: These days, it feels like there’s a major food recall (or two) each week — so much so that some crucial non-perishable ones may not have landed on your radar as you focused on whether your eggs have salmonella or if your frozen blueberries need to be thrown out. But Target’s recall of Up&Up baby wipes is one parents and other caregivers should not ignore. The retailer recalled the wipes after consumer complaints led to the Food & Drug Administration (FDA) testing them, which revealed the presence of several serious contaminants in the tested samples — critical news for anyone shopping for supplies for babies and toddlers. I spoke to Dr. Sharon Nachman, a board-certified pediatric infectious disease specialist and professor of pediatrics at Stony Brook Medicine, to find out more about the potential dangers of the contaminants. Keep reading to learn more about the specific wipes that have been recalled, along with alternatives that parents can use if baby wipes are off the changing table for them. Why were Up & Up Baby Wipes recalled? Target voluntarily recalled Up&Up Fragrance Free and Up&Up Fresh Cucumber Scented Baby Wipes after customers raised concerns about discoloration in the wipes. Following this, FDA testing identified the presence of two contaminants, Burkholderia cepacia complex and Burkholderia gladioli in samples of the wipes. The recalled products include Up&Up’s Fragrance Free Baby WIpes in 20, 72, 216, 800 and 1200 count packages with expiration dates from May 10, 2028 through November 5, 2028, along with Up&Up Fresh Cucumber Scented Baby Wipes in 72, 216 and 800 counts with expiration dates from June 29, 2028 through June 30, 2028. According to the FDA, using products contaminated with Burkholderia cepacia complex and Burkholderia gladioli can have severe and potentially life-threatening effects. The bacteria can cause skin infections even in healthy people, says Nachman, and the risk to babies is even greater. “In very young infants, like neonates, or elderly or immunocompromised populations, it’s actually much more significant and can cause sepsis and pneumonia,” she says. Newborns also often have rawer skin on their bottoms from wipes and cloths, which can also lead to mild diaper rashes that results in sensitive or broken skin in the area. “So that would allow this bacteria to enter this skin quite easily,” she says. After entering the skin, the bacteria can spread to other organs in the body, which can lead to potentially fatal sepsis or pneumonia, says Nachman. “So it’s really critical that this bacteria not be around baby skin.” What should you do if you have the recalled baby wipes? If you have the recalled wipes, the FDA says to immediately stop using them and to return them to any Target store for a full refund. You can also contact Target Guest Relations at 1-800-440-0680 for more guidance. In the future, Nachman recommends taking the following precautions when buying baby wipes to avoid potentially contaminated products: Smell the wipes, as strange or off-putting odors can be a sign of bacterial growth and contamination, she says.Check the color of the wipes. Nachman advises against using any darkened or off-color wipes, since discoloration can be a marker of potential contamination (as it was in this case with Up & Up).Consider purchasing wipes in smaller quantities. Bacteria multiplies in wet, warm environments, says Nachman, so keeping wipes in the unsealed, open packages for too long can increase the risks of bacteria growing on your wipes, so Nachman recommends buying in smaller quantities to reduce the amount of times you’re opening and closing a singular package. Alternatives to traditional baby wipes If you’re looking for alternatives to traditional baby wipes, check out the below products based on expert guidance, including top-rated options from trusted brands. Some parents prefer to use a soft wash cloth and warm water as an alternative to baby wipes, says Nachman. It can be an especially helpful alternative when you’re at home or have access to a sink and stable changing spot. These washcloths from Burt’s Bees are made from 100 percent organic cotton and have a knit terry design that’s gentle on skin and absorbent. Reviewers also like that the washcloths are durable and hold up after multiple washes. This baby body wash has the National Eczema Association’s stamp of approval for its gentle, hydrating formula that’s especially great for sensitive baby skin. The ingredients include natural oatmeal, which soothes skin, along with vitamin B5 and additional emollients for retaining moisture in the skin, according to the brand. These dry wipes are made from 100% cotton, and are gentle, fragrance-free and hypoallergenic, according to the brand.They’re made with delicate skin in mind, which is ideal for the sensitive skin on a baby’s behind. Plus they have no liquid, making them less susceptible to bacterial growth than wet, pre-moistened wipes. Meet our pediatric expert At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Dr. Sharon Nachman is a board-certified pediatric infectious disease specialist and professor of pediatrics at Stony Brook Medicine, as well as the Chief of the Division of Pediatric Infectious Disease at Stony Brook Children’s Hospital. Why trust NBC Selected? I am an associate SEO reporter for NBC Selected who’s been covering skin care, hair care and body care for over two years. I frequently report on skin care news, along with beauty deals and weekly reporting on sales and deals from prominent brands and retailers. For this piece, I researched the recall on Target’s Up&Up Baby Wipes through the FDA, and spoke to a pediatric dermatologist to find out more about what parents need to know. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: Costco shoppers challenge influencer's claim that 'insane' chicken meal can feed family of five
articles.summary: Costco's new Honey Sesame Chicken Stir Fry sparked a heated debate online after an influencer claimed the $22 prepared meal could feed as many as five people.
articles.body: A ready-to-cook Costco meal that one influencer claims can feed five people has the online community sharing their skepticism. Instagram user @costcohotfinds, who has 3.5 million followers and says she is not affiliated with the bulk grocery retailer, posted a video of herself preparing and eating Costco's new Honey Sesame Chicken Stir Fry — calling the dinner "10 out of 10" and "super kid-friendly." The meal kit contains breaded chicken, noodles, vegetables and two packets of honey sesame sauce and isn't yet available in all stores, as Tasting Table reported. SUPERMARKET HOT FOOD BARS BOOM AS AMERICANS SEEK CHEAP, EASY MEALS: HERE ARE THE TOP 3 Costco does not list the item on its website's prepared meals and foods pages, and it does not appear to have made a claim about the meal's serving size. "The amount of chicken you get in it is insane," @costcohotfinds said in her video. "This will easily feed five, and mine was only $22." The influencer noted in her narration that she baked the chicken in the oven while she cooked the noodles and vegetables on the stovetop — then topped the dish with the honey sesame sauce. "The chicken came out so crunchy," she raved. "The honey sesame sauce on this is amazing. I can't wait to have this one again — probably this weekend." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Fox News Digital reached out to Costco for comment. Those reacting to the video called the meal's serving size into question. "That would only feed my husband and my eldest son," one user commented. "I guess me and my husband identify as five people, because that would just about feed us," another person wrote, adding a laughing-face emoji. "Five? You obviously [have] never had teenagers live with you," someone else said. "Five what? A family of gerbils?" chimed in one user. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Another commenter called the meal a rip-off, saying, "You can make twice that amount at half the price if you bought the stuff to make it." "I can make it fresh at home way better and tastier and cheaper," echoed another person. "Five people on Ozempic, maybe," one user commented on a post addressing the serving-size controversy. Still, a fair share of customers pointed out that they were enthusiastic about the meal. "Oh yum!" someone wrote. "Those chicken pieces are HUGE." articles.title: Isles of Scilly Steamship Group boss resigns from role
articles.summary: Stuart Reid's last day is set to be in February after seven years in the role.
articles.body:
A ferry and airline company boss has announced he will be stepping down from his role early next year.

The Isles of Scilly Steamship Group (ISSG) said its chief executive Stuart Reid had tendered his resignation in order to take up a new job in the transport sector, with his last day set to be on 16 February 2027.

Reid has been in his current role for seven years - airline Skybus has faced criticism in recent months over its handling of services to and from the Isles of Scilly, including the cancellation of flights during the summer.

A statement from the ISSG said Reid would remain focused on delivering its priorities while the recruitment of his successor took place.

Criticism had also been made by officials in the Isles of Scilly over a deal Skybus had with Guernsey-based airline Aurigny to provide aircraft for flights to Alderney from Guernsey and Southampton.

Some suggested this agreement had exacerbated problems with Skybus flights to the Isles of Scilly.

Other issues this year have included damage to a plane and hangars at Land's End Airport during Storm Goretti, which led to delays in the firm's aircraft maintenance plans.

This combined with rising fuel costs led to Skybus axing its Newquay to London flights two months earlier than planned.

In July Jonathan Hinkles left his position as managing director of Skybus with immediate effect, with Reid taking over on an interim basis, alongside being CEO of ISSG.

ISSG thanked Reid, who worked at the company for six years before becoming chief executive, for his "commitment and leadership".

"In the meantime, it is very much business as usual, with Stuart remaining focused on delivering the group's priorities, including the integration of the Alderney operation into Skybus and the technical acceptance of Scillonian IV," a spokesperson added.

The new Isles of Scilly passenger ferry is due to come into service in March 2027 .

Councillor Steve Sims, the former lead member for transport, economy and tourism at the Council of the Isles of Scilly, said he was initially surprised to hear of Reid's resignation.

"On reflection though, he had taken an awful lot of flack recently," Sims said.

"Maybe a fresh pair of eyes would be a good thing at this stage."

Sims added he would like Reid's eventual replacement to take a longer term look at how the company operated.

He said: "They really need to look at affordability as the islands have become quite an expensive place to come to.

"People looking to travel probably end up choosing to go elsewhere as it's probably cheaper to go abroad, which means we end up losing younger visitors who are the future of the islands and of course the Steamship Company."

Andrew Sells, Visit Isles of Scilly chairman, said the tourist board wished Reid "all the best for the future".

"We look forward to continuing to work with the Steamship Company," he said.

MP Andrew George, whose St Ives constituency includes the islands, said Reid's resignation would "not calm the anxieties" of people who were concerned about lifeline transport links.

"For the chief executive to back out during a period of challenging transition will only heighten those anxieties," the Liberal Democrat said.

articles.title: Who are the ‘Hilltop Girls’ behind Israel’s ‘soft settlement’ strategy?
articles.summary: They’re not carrying out pogroms, but are nonetheless setting the stage for land grabs by Israeli settlers.
articles.body:
A radical movement of young Israeli women is leaving civilian life and education behind to live in rudimentary hilltop tents across the occupied West Bank.

Dubbed the “Hilltop Girls”, this group champions a strategy of “soft settlement”, replacing weapons and military patrols with seemingly mundane daily activities.

By portraying their presence as a natural, family-oriented social project, they aim to legitimise the gradual seizure of private Palestinian land and the establishment of new outposts.

The latest version of the ‘Hilltop Youth’

The women are in many ways an extension of the Hilltop Youth a radical religious Zionist group that emerged in 1998 when then-Israeli Foreign Minister Ariel Sharon urged settler youths to seize West Bank hilltops to preempt final status negotiations.

While the broader movement is infamous for orchestrating deadly pogroms and seizing territory by force, the female offshoot embraces an ideology geared towards establishing a “Greater Israel” that extends beyond historic Palestine to include Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and the Arabian Peninsula.

To normalise their presence, the Hilltop Girls heavily rely on social media.

Outpost accounts publish promotional videos aiming to move away from the more violent images associated with marauding Israeli settlers, who are often backed and shielded by the country’s security forces.

The female settlers claim they do not kill Palestinians or assault landowners, but merely cook and hang laundry like any other group of women.

But their end goals are similar – to establish the so-called Promised Land, including through the extension of Israel to the occupied West Bank. Their presence in the West Bank is no less illegal than that of violent extremists. And they too are transforming Palestinian pastoral land into fully-fledged settlements in violation of international law.

The Maoz Esther and Or Ahuvia outposts, located northeast of Ramallah, serve as prime examples of this systematic expansion.

Established in 2006 as a small youth outpost, Maoz Esther was demolished and rebuilt multiple times before expanding into what is now known as the “Girls’ Hill”. By 2025, it housed 17 families and more than 50 children, exceeding the size of the neighbouring 950-dunam (235-acre) Kochav HaShahar settlement.

Similarly, the Or Ahuvia outpost, established in 2023 near the Ofra settlement, reflects a broader vision to create a massive settlement bloc. The ultimate goal is to connect more than 20 outposts to Ofra, creating an integrated network capable of absorbing thousands of families in the future.

While Israeli police occasionally dismantle these outposts on camera, rights activists describe these operations as a coordinated theatrical display.

According to the Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem , most outposts enjoy direct support from the state and the army, with the women immediately rebuilding structures as soon as police depart. Logistically, these outposts are supplied with water, electricity, private road networks and military protection by the Israeli Civil Administration.

Furthermore, the government provides nearly $40m in food and clothing subsidies to Hilltop Youth members.

The movement enjoys unprecedented legislative and political cover. In early 2025, the Knesset advanced a bill proposed by the “Land of Israel” lobby to allow Jews to purchase land in the West Bank freely, ensuring these acquisitions remain protected even in the event of future political agreements.

Politicians like far-right Ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir actively support these outposts, while Defence Minister Israel Katz recently boasted to his party: “I cancelled, on my own initiative, all administrative orders against settlers in the West Bank.”

The human toll of this ideological expansion is devastating. Between January 2025 and May 2026, the United Nations recorded at least 2,806 settler attacks, averaging five incidents a day.

Prominent Hilltop Youth leader Elisha Yered recently summarised their violent strategy on a podcast, stating: “We’re very proud of initiating friction; even the army is in friction.”

In 2026 alone, systematic settler pogroms displaced nearly 2,000 Palestinians, prompting both the UN and the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs to reiterate that these relentless land grabs fundamentally undermine the possibility of a viable Palestinian state.

articles.title: Before giving away billions, MacKenzie Scott started an anti-bullying organisation; her lesser-known philanthropy cause she backed for years
articles.summary: US News: MacKenzie Scott is widely known for the extraordinary pace at which she has given away her fortune, often handing large grants to organisations with f.
articles.body: MacKenzie Scott is widely known for the extraordinary pace at which she has given away her fortune, often handing large grants to organisations with few restrictions on how the money should be spent. But years before her name became closely associated with billionaire philanthropy, she was backing a much smaller and less publicised cause.In 2014, Scott founded Bystander Revolution, an organisation focused on bullying and encouraging people to intervene when they witnessed it. The project reflected an interest in social issues that existed well before her 2019 divorce from Jeff Bezos turned her into one of the world's wealthiest women.At the time, Scott was better known as an author and the mother of four than as a major philanthropist. She had also worked at Amazon during its early years. The Bystander Revolution offered a glimpse of her charitable interests before she gained control of a vast fortune and began distributing billions of dollars to causes around the world.MacKenzie Scott's charitable journey began well before her vast fortuneScott had largely stayed out of the public spotlight during her marriage to Bezos. She was an author and mother of four, and she had also worked at Amazon during its early years, including on accounting and contract-related work. Her public profile was far smaller than that of her husband.Bystander Revolution offered a glimpse of the causes she cared about before she inherited a vast personal fortune through her 2019 divorce settlement. The organisation focused on bullying and the idea that people who witness harmful behaviour can play a role in stopping it.It was not yet the kind of large-scale philanthropy that would later define Scott's name. Her charitable interests at the time also included issues such as marriage equality, housing for homeless families and scholarships for undocumented students brought to the US as children.Scott's biggest philanthropic chapter began with a life-changing settlementScott's life changed dramatically in 2019 when her marriage to Bezos ended. As part of the divorce settlement, she received a substantial Amazon stake, giving her a fortune of a scale that few people ever control.Rather than simply holding on to that wealth, she quickly began discussing how she intended to distribute it.In May 2019, Scott signed the Giving Pledge, promising to give away at least half of her wealth during her lifetime or in her will. Her pledge went further than a conventional promise to donate. She wrote that she would continue giving until her "safe" was emptyHer Giving Pledge reflected a philanthropy model built on trust and unrestricted fundsScott's later philanthropy became striking not simply because of its size, but because of how little control she sought over the organisations receiving it.Instead of creating a traditional foundation with a large bureaucracy and extensive grant-making process, she increasingly favoured unrestricted donations. The idea was simple: organisations working on the ground often know better than a wealthy donor how money should be spent.Her philosophy was captured in her Giving Pledge letter. Scott wrote about the danger of saving resources for some supposedly better moment in the future and argued for acting on the impulse to give.She gave billions without taking controlAccording to a Forbes report, by July 2020, Scott had already announced approximately $1.7 billion in donations to 116 organisations. The recipients worked across areas including racial and gender equity, economic mobility, public health, climate change and other social issues.As reported in the Forbes 2022 report, Scott had given $8.6 billion to 780 organisations. The grants covered a wide range of causes, while the organisations themselves were generally given considerable freedom over how to use the money.In 2023, Harvard Business School researchers described Scott as one of the most influential figures in philanthropy and highlighted the speed of her giving and her willingness to give up control with $15 billion in 5 years.The anti-bullying work adds another side to her storyScott did not suddenly begin engaging with social causes after becoming one of the world's wealthiest women. The anti-bullying organisation she founded years earlier shows that philanthropy and social issues were already part of her public work.Her later giving simply operated on a vastly different scale. The transformation was remarkable. A woman who had once maintained a relatively low profile became a major force in global philanthropy almost immediately after receiving her share of the Amazon fortune.From a quiet organisation to a new model of givingScott's anti-bullying work and her later philanthropy may look very different on the surface. One was a focused organisation built around a specific social problem. The other involves billions of dollars distributed across thousands of nonprofits and causes.But there is a thread connecting them: a willingness to put resources behind people and organisations trying to address social problems.That became particularly clear in Scott's later philosophy. Rather than positioning herself as the person with all the answers, she has generally argued that the organisations doing the work should have the freedom to decide what they need.The Giving Pledge remains a useful marker of that shift. When Scott made her promise in 2019, she did not announce a detailed blueprint for spending her fortune. Instead, she emphasised acting rather than waiting.The result has made her one of the most consequential individual donors of her generation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: RuPaul's Drag Race UK welcomes the "Ru Generation"
articles.summary: A new wave of queens raised on the hit reality show are among the 12 contestants set to compete for the series eight crown.
articles.body:
A new batch of queens from across the UK are set to battle it out in the hope of hearing RuPaul's magical words: "Condragulations, you're a winner, baby".

The UK edition of Drag Race has been putting hopeful contestants through their paces for seven years - plenty of time for a new wave of talent raised on the hit reality show to emerge.

Now "Generation Ru" are ready to compete for the crown and £25,000 cash prize.

Series eight contestant Mocha, 26, tells BBC Newsbeat she considers herself part of this new cohort.

"My drag has always been inspired by Drag Race because that's why I started," the Essex-born queen says.

"I think watching Drag Race made me realise that all of these things that I grew up wanting to do - like be a fashion designer, be a singer, like be a dancer, do makeup - it's actually all these things combined and I can be all of them at once."

Mocha, who describes herself as a "fashion clown" and musical theatre lover, says it has taken her nearly a decade to get to this stage but feels it is the "right time".

And while watching the show has influenced her style and given her a something to work towards, she says the process isn't for those who just want to get on TV.

"Drag is hard and you've got to love it, you've got to have a passion for it," she says.

"Drag Race is the extra-special prize you get at the end, but it's not the main goal in that way."

London-based queen and fellow contestant Flesh agrees she is "100% Generation Ru".

"I found drag through queens who had featured in the American franchise," the 26-year-old says.

"And from the first season of the UK franchise I was hooked, I was a fan.

"It has always really been my blueprint.“

She has also developed her "supermodel of Soho" style alongside her best friend Bones, the reigning Drag Race UK Superstar.

Flesh says she was "so happy" for her drag sister when she won, but it also made her "terrified" to compete this year as she focused on proving herself.

Almost 100 queens have lip-synced their way through Drag Race UK's challenges, but there are fans who worry whether the British scene can support more series of the annual show.

Series eight's youngest contestant, Naya Thorn, who was 23 when she was chosen for the show, feels there are new queens cropping up all over the UK.

But she admits the show would benefit if more "seasoned and colourful characters" from across the scene got involved.

However, she says, cost-of-living pressures are putting a strain on queens trying to make it.

Naya, from Dudley, West Midlands, says the expense of preparing for the show almost led her to drop-out, and she wouldn't have been TV-ready without her support network at home.

"It really upsets me that there's a lot of people that would do well on the show and should have that platform that feel like they can't go on because of how expensive it seems to be getting," she says.

"But I am here to prove to everyone, you don't need that much money."

Flesh, who has been running a drag show for the past five years, says she has also seen turnout at live performances drop, and feels soaring costs have likely impacted that.

She thinks the TV show still appeals as it provides "the joy and the power of drag from the comfort of your own home", but says this comes at a price to performers.

"Expectations remain at a Drag Race level and our income and opportunities in the real world do not reflect that," she says.

The Soho-based queen also says social media has become a "double-edged sword".

Although it's vital to advertise live shows, "the more you show... the less inclined people are to go", she says.

Flesh adds: "If the public aren't willing to support drag outside of the Drag Race vehicle" then "we won't be able to sustain Drag Race".

The queens this year will be hoping to spark more interest into the show and drag, including Paris Baby, who describes herself as "UK's British Bajan Barbie".

She has been hailing the new series as the "drag renaissance" as she feels it was a "really strong" year and hopes it will be "very well received" internationally.

"Hopefully we can bring a little 'je ne sais quoi' and reignite the interest in drag," she says.

articles.title: Cancelled ferry service causes issues for Guernsey sports clubs
articles.summary: Sports clubs have said the suspension of a ferry service between the islands has "caused problems".
articles.body:
Sports clubs have said the suspension of a passenger ferry service between Jersey and Guernsey has "caused problems".

Islands Unlimited suspended its service until 10 September following a "major failure" to the MV San Pawl's starboard main engine.

Guernsey Cricket said it has had to charter boats to Jersey in order to compete in upcoming matches.

The club's chief operating officer Richard Headington said it was "dependent on the ferry" and had to spent a "significant amount of extra money" to cover the charter costs.

Headington said chartering boats was the most "economical alternative" but the cancellation of the service caused a "bit of a panic".

He said the club used the ferry service "quite extensively" with many sides travelling between the islands over the summer.

He added that the club may look to plan a "contingency plan" in the future.

Emily Squire, president of the Guernsey Triathlon Club said the ferry service was "key" and "we are a bit stuck without it".

The club is set to host Jersey Tri Club athletes for the Granite Weekender on Saturday and Sunday, the biggest triathlon it offers with about 30 athletes expected to travel.

She said the athletes could not fly over with their bikes and the "smaller boat charters cost more money so it does make you wonder whether the competitions can go ahead".

Squire said the club had received support.

"Brittany Ferries have offered to bring everyone's bikes over and Bailiwick Boat Charters will do two runs to bring all the athletes over, so all the athletes are going to make it."

Islands Unlimited said the suspension of the ferry service was introduced to ensure the "safety of passengers, crew and the vessel".

It apologised and thanked people for their "patience and understanding", adding every affected booking would receive a full refund.

articles.title: US draws a red line on PM Modi’s Iran meeting
articles.summary: US News: TOI correspondent from Washington: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has sought to draw a red line between India’s right to conduct its own diplomacy .
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has sought to draw a red line between India’s right to conduct its own diplomacy and Washington’s determination to prevent Iran from rebuilding the economic lifelines strangled by US sanctions.“I don’t think there’s a trade deal between India and Iran,” Rubio said Wednesday, after PM Narendra Modi’s meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan drew scrutiny in Washington DC. But he followed that reassurance with a warning that was plainly less accommodating: countries should not help Tehran create mechanisms to generate revenue that could finance terrorism or its nuclear programme, and those that do could themselves face US sanctions.The timing of Rubio’s warning, coming on the heels of PM Modi's meeting with Pezeshkian, made the message to New Delhi – which prides itself on its independent foreign policy – difficult to miss. The two leaders discussed expanding and diversifying bilateral trade, the wars and instability in West Asia, and the need to protect freedom of navigation and commercial shipping after attacks in the region killed Indian seafarers. India described the meeting as “fruitful” but no formal trade agreement was announced. Pezeshkian, for his part, is reported to have asked PM Modi to use India's extensive diplomatic contacts to encourage dialogue and help end the conflict.For New Delhi, Iran is not simply another diplomatic relationship; it is a strategic geographic bridge. Iran's Chabahar port gives India a route into Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan, while the International North-South Transport Corridor offers a potential land-and-sea connection from India through Iran to Russia and wider Eurasia. Iran has also traditionally been an important source of energy for India. Such interests explain why New Delhi has repeatedly sought exemptions and accommodations from Washington over Chabahar even as US sanctions have made commercial dealings increasingly hazardous.The Bishkek summit also gave Iran a larger diplomatic stage at a particularly vulnerable moment for Tehran. Pezeshkian met Russian President Vladimir Putin, thanking Moscow for its support and calling for closer cooperation against what he described as US “unilateralism.” He also met Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.Yet his message was not simply defiance. Addressing the SCO, he said Iran was prepared to reciprocate if Washington honoured commitments under an interim agreement reached in June, and indicated that Tehran remained open to negotiations. He also linked freedom of navigation through the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz to implementation of the agreement.The SCO meeting -- largely ignored by the US media -- itself provided Tehran with diplomatic company at a critical time. Its members condemned the military strikes on Iran and rejected unilateral coercive measures, while reaffirming Iran's right to peaceful nuclear activity. The organisation also called for greater cooperation in energy, trade and finance. "This is a big deal, particularly since India - an ally of both the US and Israel - also signed it," noted Trita Parsi, a foreign policy analyst with the Quincy Institute for Responsible StatecrafIn Washington, that is precisely what makes the SCO uncomfortable. American commentators see it less as a coherent anti-US alliance than as evidence of an emerging world in which countries increasingly want freedom from American economic and diplomatic dominance. Western analysts, however, don’t view India's participation as allying with the China-Russia axis; rather, New Delhi is seen as using overlapping institutions to maximise its room for manoeuvre.India now sits at an extraordinary number of geopolitical tables: the US-led Quad with Japan and Australia; the BRICS grouping, which it chairs this year; the SCO alongside China, Russia and Iran; and the G20, which will meet in Florida later this year, besides other regional and Global South forums. To Washington, this is simultaneously an asset and an irritation. India is an increasingly important US partner in balancing China — but it refuses to become an American ally in the traditional sense.For New Delhi, the logic is a no-brainer: partnership with US does not require hostility toward Russia, China or Iran. But the space for that multi-alignment is narrowing rapidly in MAGA's America First era. With Washington intensifying secondary sanctions against anyone helping Tehran generate revenue – and even the UAE curbing its economic channels with Iran – Indian companies, banks and shippers face the real cost of India's diplomatic balancing act. PM Modi may continue to meet everyone; the harder question is how long Indian business can afford to do the same.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trey Gowdy opens up about the hidden toll of becoming a great prosecutor
articles.summary: Trey Gowdy reveals the emotional toll of his prosecutorial career and recalls encounters with David Smith from the infamous Susan Smith murder case.
articles.body: For Trey Gowdy, the best prosecutors don't simply prove their case, they make a jury feel it themselves. "The best prosecutors are the ones that can make the jury feel what the parents feel," Gowdy said on the latest episode of the "Hang Out With Sean Hannity" podcast. "And that's what takes its toll. It wrecks you. It wrecks you," he added. HOW TO WATCH THE 'HANG OUT WITH SEAN HANNITY' PODCAST Gowdy, now a Fox News host, sat down with Hannity for a wide-ranging conversation reflecting on the skills and emotional toll behind a prosecutorial career in which he never lost a case. For Gowdy, connecting with a jury meant first finding a way to understand the anguish of the people at the center of a case. "Having children helps because you imagine, what if they were taken from you? Having a spouse helps," Gowdy said. "But some folks, I think either are born with or can acquire this empathetic gene, where they can communicate that anguish and pain." But one case he recalled offered an especially haunting reminder of the grief that remains long after a prosecution ends. FATHER RECALLS HORROR AFTER SON MURDERED HIS 5 GRANDCHILDREN: ‘I KNEW HE KILLED THEM’ He recalled regularly encountering David Smith, whose two young sons were drowned by their mother, Susan Smith, in a notorious 1994 South Carolina murder case. "The father of those two boys worked at the grocery store where I shopped, Saturday mornings," Gowdy said. "And I made a point of always speaking to him and never mentioning the case. We talked sports." "But if you want to see grief etched in someone's face, it was etched in his," he continued. "To lose your two sons because your wife decided that she wanted to have a different boyfriend." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The encounters with Smith offered Gowdy a firsthand glimpse of the anguish he says prosecutors must somehow convey to jurors while remaining composed enough to make their case. "You've got to marshal the evidence, you've got to stay composed long enough to prevent it, and then this marriage of logic and passion is what closing argument is, this marriage, of moving people," he added. articles.title: Joanna Lumley joins Blackheath vigil for Nepal flood victims
articles.summary: The actress, who has ties to the country, said she was heartbroken by the deadly flood on 26 August.
articles.body:
Dame Joanna Lumley has shared her belief that the "heartbreaking" flash flood in Nepal was caused by human behaviour and climate change, as she joined a vigil in south-east London to remember the victims.

About 50 people gathered at Panas Gurkha Restaurant in Blackheath on Thursday to observe a minute's silence, light candles and hold prayers.

The actress, who has frequently visited Nepal and has strong ties with the Gurkha community, said the flood in the north of the country on 26 August could have been predicted.

Nepal's foreign ministry said 1,252 deaths had been recorded since the flood and 4,200 people remained missing, including 590 foreign nationals.

On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield told the House of Lords that 36 British people were currently unaccounted for, up from the previous total of 33.

During the vigil, Dame Joanna said: "I think... around the world our hearts have been absolutely broken by what happened in Nepal.

"The sense that it could have maybe been predicted by all the people who understood that by human activities somehow the world seems to be changing, seems to be getting warmer.

"These catastrophes, the great Himalayan glaciers melting, isn't something that we haven't heard of and thought of before.

"When you see the catastrophic outcome, I think we feel completely hopeless every day we look in the papers."

The United States Geological Survey (USGS) said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event struck near the border between Nepal and China.

It added that a "glacial collapse and debris flow" caused "subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream".

Rescue efforts had previously been hampered by fears of more flooding from a lake formed by the glacier collapse which sparked the flooding.

Dame Joanna said having visited and travelled in the country, "it breaks my heart because I know how difficult it is to get around".

"It seems that we have been warned about this over the years," she added.

"I do believe that what we do here, and the fossil fuels we burn and the plastic waste in the sea and so on, I do believe that is making the world a sicker place and a weaker place.

"And the places which are melting fastest are the high mountains and places, and so the Himalayas are there."

Dame Joanna is the patron of healthcare charity Doctors for Nepal and vice patron of The Gurkha Welfare Trust, which provides aid to Gurkha veterans who served in the British Army.

Her father served in the 6th Gurkha Rifles, a regiment of the British Indian Army, during the Second World War.

Vice Lord-Lieutenant Colonel Jane Davis, former Coronation Street star Sally Lindsay, drummer Steve White and Greenwich mayor David Wardrop also joined the vigil.

articles.title: New GP and wellbeing hub in Newhavan 'a major milestone'
articles.summary: The £21m hub brings together primary care, community wellbeing and leisure services in one location.
articles.body:
A cluster of empty and under‑used buildings in East Sussex has been transformed into a £21m modern health hub.

Wellbeing Square in Newhaven, which brings together primary care, community wellbeing and leisure services in one location, officially opened on Thursday.

The project was led by Lewes District Council, which said it would "deliver a high‑quality, modern healthcare environment that residents so richly deserve".

Council leader Zoe Nicholson called the venue a "major milestone in the history of the town".

"Not only is it transformational for people living in Newhaven but is also central to our wider regeneration plans," she said.

The completed scheme includes two state‑of‑the‑art GP practices, a new pharmacy, an extension to Seahaven Swim & Fitness Centre operated by Wave Active, and a creative/co‑working space.

The council says the plan is to create an environment which can offer healthcare, wellbeing and community services delivered side‑by‑side.

The two GP surgeries combined will serve more than 15,000 local residents, with more than 5.500 appointments offered on the site each month.

Dr Paul Moore, a GP at Quayside Medical Practice, said: "We are encouraging people to be as healthy as they can."

He says the new hub will reinforce the message that "your GP is there for you".

Allison Cannon, chief nursing officer for NHS Sussex and Surrey, says the new hub will make it easier for people to access support closer to home and at a convenient time.

"This is exactly the kind of neighbourhood approach we want to see more of across Surrey and Sussex," she said.

"It's where health services, local partners and communities come together to help people stay well, tackle health inequalities and support healthier lives."

articles.title: How a fly brain may help explain the secrets of human behaviour
articles.summary: Comparing the brains of male and female flies may transform our understanding of how genes shape behaviour, including ours.
articles.body:
Scientists have managed to compare the fine detail of the brains of male and female flies for the first time, identifying differences they say explain male aggression, courtship and their singing of love songs.

The scientists in Cambridge mapped all 124 million connections of nerve cells in a male fly's brain, having done the same for a female fly two years ago.

The team are clear that the research won't explain differences between men and women because our behaviour is far more complex.

But the research could help scientists better understand human behaviour and conditions in which genetic differences affect brain wiring, such as autism and schizophrenia.

Prof Gregory Jefferis, of the Medical Research Council's Laboratory of Molecular Biology and University of Cambridge, who co-led the research, told BBC News that the breakthrough was "a really important new avenue in neuroscience", likening it to the invention of a powerful new telescope in increasing our understanding of the Universe.

"We have this amazing stuff in our heads that lets us do incredible things such as playing a sonata or solving a scientific problem. And this development could help our understanding of how those systems work".

The fly's brain is as beautiful as it is incredible. It is the size of a pin head – yet in many ways - more efficient than a supercomputer and able to outsmart the smartest AI.

Jefferis' team and collaborators painstakingly analysed every nerve cell, every wire and every connection in a male fruit fly. They put them together into a 3D map of the brain and nerve cord and compared them to the earlier, female mapping.

They found that around 95% of the cells are shared between the male and female fly brains. But the remaining 5% are enough to drive quite distinct behaviours, according to Dr Isabella Beckett, who is joint first author of the scientific research paper published today in the Journal Cell.

"We were expecting to find differences, and we found them, and we're excited by what we got," she said.

The small differences they discovered can lead to big changes in behaviour.

In courtship, for example, the male tracks the female as she moves. The researchers have identified the brain circuits associated with that trait and found key differences in the wiring. The males have extra bits that should enhance his visual tracking.

There is an even bigger difference in the circuits associated with aggression. Males fight more often and so there is much more wiring associated with that behaviour than in females.

And then, there is the love song circuit.

Males woo females by producing a sound. They have wiring unique only to them to producee the sound. According to Dr Philipp Schlegel, co-author of the study, the circuit has to be just right, otherwise the consequneces for the poor male could be dire.

"The courtship also includes singing to the female," he told me. "The sound is produced by vibrating the wings to produce a very specific song.

"If the female likes it, she will allow him to approach, and if she doesn't, and she's not receptive at a time, she'll basically reject him, which could be a kick to the face".

These three differences between male and female wiring in flies are driven by two key genes. Researchers have known about the genes for years, and how they're linked to each of these behaviours. What they've never been able to see is the bit in the middle. Now, for the first time, they can see the actual wiring those genes produce.

The primary aim of the research was not to discover the differences between male and female flies, and certainly not to find neurological explanations for certain alleged behavioural differences between men and women.

Comparing two brains that have some slight wiring differences associated with known big behavioural differences enables scientists to clearly see the principles that underlie the changes to brain wiring for all behaviour, according to Beckett.

"You just have one independent variable, the sex, and then you can see what's different. This is a scientist's dream".

These differences take scientists a big step forward in understanding one of the biggest questions in biology - how genes influence behaviour.

Scientists have known for decades that they do, but have had little idea of exactly how they exert their influence. The answer, according to Dr Jefferis, is in how the genes shape the brain's wiring and how that wiring influences behaviour.

"The fly brain comparison gives us a really good handle on this," he told BBC News.

"There are patterns of behaviour in humans that seem to have a strong genetic, basis. So, for example, there are many gene varients now related to schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorders that we don't really understand".

There are also possible applications in improving AI and boosting computer systems, he adds.

"To have AI that's efficient as, as our brains, is probably going to take more biological inspiration. And the inspiration that's likely to be important is actually real biological wiring diagrams.

"There are people who've been putting the fly brain in the middle of artificial networks and trying to see if it's useful to help, learn and control artificial systems".

Other scientific collaborators were from the HHMI Janelia Research Campus led by Prof Gerry Rubin, Drosophila Connectomics Group at the University of Cambridge, Google Research and the Champalimaud Foundation

articles.title: Four imprisoned Palestine Action activists appeal ‘terrorism’ sentences
articles.summary: Supporters of those who participated in a raid on an Israeli weapons maker say the sentences set a dangerous precedent.
articles.body:
London, the UK – Four Palestine Action activists who were sentenced as “terrorists” are appealing against the ruling.

Charlotte Head, Samuel Corner, Leona Kamio, and Fatema Zainab Rajwani were found guilty of criminal damage “with a terrorist connection” following a raid, which was claimed by Palestine Action, on an Israeli arms factory in August 2024 in Filton, near Bristol.

The sentencing marked the first categorisation of property damage as “terrorism” in British courts.

Human rights groups condemned the ruling in June.

“Uncontested, this judgement will also mark a flagrant departure from the rule of law in favour of foreign criminal actors and against and in the detriment of UK citizens,” said Shahd Hammouri, lecturer in international law and researcher of corporate war profiteering at the University of Kent, as she spoke on Thursday during a press conference in London, where supporters of the group announced the appeal.

“It will also set out a precedent that may extend to others who are protesting against grave violations of international law.”

At the time of the incident, Palestine Action was not a proscribed organisation.

Activists Head and Kamio were handed five-year sentences, while Corner, who was also convicted of grievous bodily harm without intent for striking a police officer during the raid, was given seven years and eight months. Rajwani, who at 21 is the youngest of the group, was handed a sentence of four years and eight months.

The appeal argues that the conviction violated Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), as Palestine Action was not a proscribed organisation at the time of the offence. It also argues that “the sentences were manifestly excessive” and violated the “principles of natural justice” as well as ECHR’s Article 6, which regards the right to a fair trial.

The mothers of Kamio and Rajwani, visibly emotional when describing prison conditions and futures their children may face, said they were proud of their daughters.

“She may be embroiled in this struggle for her freedom for another 20 years,” said Sukaina Rajwani.

Emma Kamio’s voice broke when stating, “[Leona] will be 50 years old…when she finishes her sentence”, referring to the decades of supervision that would follow time spent in prison.

Elbit Systems, Palestine Action’s main target, describes its drones as the “backbone” of the Israeli army.

The August 2024 Filton raid was carried out at its UK affiliate.

Palestine Action says it is “committed to ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime”. The group relies on direct action to disrupt flows of arms and military-related goods to Israel, stating that “If one action stops one weapon from killing a Palestinian, then it’s all worth it.”

James Smith, a doctor who returned eight days ago from Gaza, where he was providing urgent medical care, said it was “an honour” to support the activists.

Direct action efforts should be “understood alongside the sheer inability of healthcare workers to respond to the outcomes of these war machines”, he said, referring to Israeli quadcopter drones.

He referenced the shooting of a 10-month-old baby in Gaza by an Israeli quadcopter in April, 2024.

The activists known as the “Filton 24” have said they were targeting quadcopter drones produced by Elbit Systems during their raid.

When speaking of the activists, Smith noted the “first tenet” of medical best practice, saying, “Prevention is better than cure.”

People sentenced as “terrorists” are treated as dangerous and face scrutiny long after they leave prison.

Kamio said her daughter had worked with children at a nursery, facilitating outdoor, nature-based learning. While the nursery spoke highly of her, her mother said she feared that once released, she would not be able to work with children again because of enhanced checks.

In a statement, activists supporting the four said that they “would be subject to notification requirements for 15 years upon release” and that “such requirements include being obliged to notify police of any new device, bank account, address, holiday or relationship”.

In June, the case gained further prominence when Head’s lawyer, Rajiv Menon KC, was accused by Justice Jeremy Johnson of contempt of court by stating that Elbit Systems was “wined and dined in the corridors of power” and reminded jurors of their right to acquit based on conscience.

Menon now faces contempt proceedings; senior lawyers have criticised his prosecution.

“[Judge] Johnson did his worst,” Emma Kamio said of the sentencing.

In June 2025 , the UK banned Palestine Action as “terrorist” organisation, making it a crime to be a member of or to express support for the group. More than 2,700 people have been arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 for protesting the ban.

The proscription, which came after activists spray-painted a Royal Air Force plane, placed Palestine Action on par with organisations like al-Qaeda, ISIL (ISIS) and extreme far-right groups.

Civil liberty organisations and United Nations experts have slammed the ban as an illiberal overreach.

Charlotte Head, in a letter written from prison, described the sentencing as “politically motivated to justify the proscription of Palestine Action”.

There is no date set for when the appeal will be heard, but lawyer Simon Natas said he hoped it would begin “in the coming months”.

articles.title: In the shadow of Clancy case, U.K. treatment of postpartum psychosis wins supporters
articles.summary: Sofii Lewis believes that had she not received treatment within the U.K.’s trailblazing maternal mental healthcare system after being diagnosed with “tendencies of postpartum psychosis,” both she and Evie might not be alive today.
articles.body: LONDON — Sofii Lewis knew something was deeply wrong within days of giving birth to her first child, Evie, in January 2023. “I just didn’t have a bond with my daughter,” Lewis said. “I didn’t really want to be around her.” Then the part-time baker became convinced that she or someone else might harm Evie. At night, a beeping sound — like that of a checkout till — haunted Lewis. She began to fear that someone was going to “buy Evie,” and she became “very suicidal,” said Lewis, who is now 27. She also began to have thoughts of taking Evie’s life, in addition to her own. “I know I certainly was hours, days away,” said Lewis, who lives in Aberdare, Wales. Lewis believes that had she not received treatment within the U.K.’s trailblazing maternal mental healthcare system after being diagnosed with “tendencies of postpartum psychosis,” both she and Evie might not be alive today. Lewis and other mothers she knows who have experienced maternal mental health struggles have been closely watching the case of Lindsay Clancy, who has been on trial for killing her three children after strangling them in their Duxbury, Massachusetts home in January 2023. Clancy’s defense team has argued that she should not be held criminally responsible for her actions because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time. “A lot of other mums I’m in contact with who had postpartum psychosis also find it very, very triggering,” Lewis, whose daughter was born the same month that Clancy killed her three children, said of the case. “Because that could have been any one of us who did that.” It was receiving months of care at a Mother and Baby Unit that Lewis says may have saved both her and Evie’s lives. MBUs are specialist, inpatient units that treat women suffering from mental health issues during pregnancy and after the birth of their children in the U.K. That the service allows mothers to remain with their babies as they receive care instead of being separated deserves to be emulated elsewhere, experts and mothers say. “I strongly believe if she’d been in the U.K., she would have been admitted to a Mother and Baby Unit and all three of her kids would still be alive today — and she would be absolutely fine,” Lewis said of Clancy. ‘Cradle’ of modern maternal healthcare Veerle Bergink, a psychiatrist, said she agreed that Clancy’s case might have ended differently had she been treated at one of the U.K.’s National Health Service MBUs. “Lindsay Clancy had a severe postpartum mental illness,” said Bergink, who is the Director of Mount Sinai’s Women’s Mental Health Center in New York. “And she did not get the right treatment.” The U.K., she said, is considered by many in the field as “the cradle” of modern maternal mental healthcare.” Meanwhile, the U.S. “is behind in knowledge about perinatal psychiatry,” with limited options for treatment for serious conditions like postpartum psychosis in America’s fragmented healthcare system, she said. According to Bergink, Britain’s MBU approach is “without a doubt” the best way to treat postpartum psychosis. According to the National Health Service, or NHS, up to 26% of new and expectant mothers experience perinatal mental health illness, which covers a wide range of conditions. In 2025 alone, it says on its website that more than 66,000 women accessed specialist community-based care and support for perinatal mental health issues. Symptoms of postpartum psychosis, which falls under that umbrella, can start within the first two weeks after birth, or later. Symptoms and their severity can vary widely and include delusions, hallucinations, mania, confusion and other signs. Suicide linked to the condition is rare and infanticide is even rarer, emphasizes Action on Postpartum Psychosis, or APP, a British charity. Of around 1,200 cases of postpartum psychosis identified in the U.K. each year, around 1 to 5 are linked to cases of suicide, according to the organization. In the decade up to 2021, less than 0.05% resulted in infanticide, it said, though it noted that the exact numbers can be difficult to quantify. Clancy’s defense team outlined how she had repeatedly sought mental health care, including seeing psychiatrists, calling a suicide hotline and being hospitalized, before fatally strangling her three children and then trying to take her own life. Prosecutors argue that she took deliberate and premeditated steps to kill her children and was aware that her actions were wrong. The jury in her trial has been deadlocked for five days and was due to resume deliberations on Thursday. Her trial has drawn international attention and sparked an unprecedented dialogue in the U.S. around postpartum psychosis and the need for better access to maternal mental healthcare. Lewis said she shared her symptoms with a private counsellor whom she had sought support from in the past. Her counsellor acted swiftly to contact a crisis team within the National Health Service, or the NHS, the U.K.’s public healthcare system, and within days Lewis and Evie were admitted to a Mother and Baby Unit. Lewis said the care she received within the MBU over the course of five months likely saved both of their lives. According to Bergink, the MBU approach is “without a doubt” the best way to treat postpartum psychosis. ‘Incredible progress’ While some countries have similar inpatient programming for mothers suffering maternal mental health issues, the scale of Britain’s MBU program is “pretty unique to the U.K.,” Dr. Sally Wilson, the National Training Coordinator for APP, said in a phone interview Wednesday, with the NHS, she said, making “incredible progress, particularly over the last 10 years” in addressing the realities of postpartum psychosis. There are about 20 units in England, with at least two in Scotland and one in Wales, according to APP, which has been campaigning for the expansion of the program. While a handful of countries have similar programming, Wilson said few initiatives are as comprehensive as the U.K.’s. In the U.S. there is no nationwide system offering inpatient care for mothers and babies comparable to the U.K.’s network of MBUs, though some hospitals and clinics do offer specialized perinatal psychiatric care. Wilson, who joined APP after receiving what she described as lifesaving support from the organization during her own struggle with postpartum psychosis, said the development of the MBU program stemmed from prominent perinatal psychiatrists, as well as survivors, advocating for more awareness and specified treatment for the condition, as well as for broader maternal mental healthcare. Treatment plans within MBUs can vary and can include medication, with patients sometimes spending weeks to months at the facilities. Lewis, who now volunteers with APP as a peer supporter, said she benefited from two particular therapies during her treatment in particular, including Video Interaction Guidance, or VIG, therapy, in which video is captured of a parent interacting with their baby to be played back, highlighting the positive moments of connection they have with their infant. She said she also benefited from Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing, or EMDR, therapy, a treatment designed to alleviate the distress associated with trauma. Once the two were discharged, she continued to receive care through a perinatal community team and recovered from her symptoms day by day. Still, both Lewis and Wilson say that there is much work to be done, both in the U.K. and around the world, raise awareness around the realities and signs of postpartum psychosis, as well as a need for greater resources for and access to maternal mental healthcare, including to MBUs Lewis said she wanted survivors of postpartum psychosis to know, “it doesn’t make you a bad person.” “It doesn’t make you a bad mum, a bad wife, a bad partner,” she said. “It’s just part of the illness that you have at that time.” If you are pregnant or a new mother and you are in crisis, the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline provides free, confidential support 24/7 in English and Spanish. Call or text the hotline at 1-833-852-6262 If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7, to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit
