articles.title: Panama Canal restricts traffic amid Hormuz crisis: Why this matters
articles.summary: Limits on the number of vessels in the canal could create shipping delays and increase freight costs.
articles.body:
While shipping remains severely disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz, shippers are facing new constraints at another strategic maritime chokepoint on the other side of the world: the Panama Canal.

From this week, the number of vessels permitted to pass through the canal per day will begin to fall because of low water levels, canal authorities say.

Here’s what we know about the latest measures at the canal, which handles some 5 percent of global maritime trade , according to the Panama Canal authority.

What restrictions are being introduced in the Panama Canal?

From Thursday, only 34 vessels will be permitted to sail daily through the canal, which has traditionally been able to accommodate up to 40 per day.

On September 15, the cap will drop further to 32.

The Panama Canal Authority, the body which oversees the waterway, says the new limits are necessary as the country braces for lower water levels due to the El Nino weather phenomenon .

In the area of the canal, rainfall from May to August is down by 34 percent from its historical average, the authority said, adding that El Nino could cut it even more.

The authority has already implemented other water conservation measures, such as lowering the maximum draft – the vessel’s depth in the water – for the largest ships.

How significant is the Panama Canal for world trade?

Some $270bn of cargo passed through the canal in 2024, according to research by Al Jazeera. The passageway accounted for 40 percent of all US container traffic and 2.5 percent of all global sea trade.

This year, according to the Panama Canal authority, that has risen to 5 percent of all global sea trade, with 70 percent destined for or originating in the US.

Has traffic in the Panama Canal been increasing this year?

At the end of June, Panama Canal administrator Ricaurte Vasquez Morales said more than 10,000 vessels had transited the canal over the previous nine months, up 5.2 percent from the same period a year earlier, driven largely by increases in container ships and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) carriers.

He also said the canal’s total vessel tonnage was 7.2 percent higher during the same period.

How has the Hormuz crisis contributed to this?

With Gulf producers unable to export as much oil through the Strait of Hormuz as they did before the war – about 20 million barrels of oil per day (bpd) – countries are increasingly turning to North and South America to make up supplies, driving more traffic towards the Panama Canal.

The effect has been particularly pronounced for crude oil exports from the United States, which leapt by 46 percent year-on-year to a record 61.6 million metric tonnes in the second quarter of 2026, according to global trade intelligence firm Kpler – equivalent to about 450 million barrels in total, or an average of about 5 million bpd.

Brazil, Argentina and Guyana have all posted record shipments of oil so far in 2026.

What impact will the new Panama restrictions have?

The rise in cargoes needing to be shipped through the canal is already creating a bidding war for transit slots in the canal.

While average auction prices for transit slots were $55,000 between October last year and February this year, the recent surge in demand has caused those prices to jump three-fold, according to the canal’s authority.

One South Korean ship paid a record $5.3m to pass through the canal on September 1, according to Bloomberg News.

Niels Rasmussen, chief shipping analyst at the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO), an international shipping association, said the canal’s new restrictions will put more pressure on shipping, pushing some vessels to reroute and make longer, more costly journeys around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.

“Reduced cargo capacity, combined with higher auction prices for transit slots, is likely to push freight rates higher,” Rasmussen told Al Jazeera.

Container cargo moving from Asia to the US’s east coast, as well as LPG exports from the US Gulf to Asia and the western coasts of Central and South America, could be particularly affected, he added.

articles.title: Indonesia: Around 2,000 fall ill after eating free school meals
articles.summary: Authorities are investigating several suspected outbreaks amid growing criticism of the scheme.
articles.body:
Around 2,000 students and teachers across Indonesia have fallen ill with food poisoning over the past three days linked to the government's free school meals programme.

In the latest case, 777 people became unwell after consuming the food at a high school in Rembang, Central Java, the institution's headteacher said.

The meals were provided through a multibillion-dollar scheme that is one of President Prabowo Subianto's signature policies, aiming to improve nutrition for Indonesia's schoolchildren.

But, as well as being the suspected source of a string of mass food poisonings, the programme has been dogged by allegations of corruption and criticism of its cost.

A total of 752 students and 25 teachers experienced symptoms of food poisoning after eating meals provided through the Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG) programme at the high school in Lasem on Wednesday lunchtime.

"They had diarrhoea and took turns using the toilet," headteacher Juhartutik told BBC News Indonesia. "There are 40 toilets in total, so they can't accommodate everyone."

The school has since sent nearly 1,200 pupils and 95 members of staff home, while several were taken to hospital.

Juhartutik said the government would cover any medical costs and that the local food distributor had come to the school to "take responsibility".

The suspected outbreak came after 730 people fell ill after consuming MBG meals at an Islamic boarding school in Sidoarjo, East Java, on Tuesday, a local health official said.

Reni said their child felt dizzy and nauseous before developing stomach problems after eating the meal.

Some of those affected required hospital treatment, with some students being transported in wheelchairs because they were too weak to stand.

Hundreds of others have been affected by suspected cases of food poisoning linked to the free school meals this week, including hundreds across several schools in Tana Toraja, South Sulawesi.

Improper storage or poorly prepared food are often to blame for cases of food poisoning, in which the body rejects the contaminated food.

Parents and teachers have told reporters of slimy chicken, as well as food that appeared undercooked and had a fishy odour.

Local authorities are investigating the cause of the suspected outbreaks, with food samples being tested for possible contamination.

The head of the food distribution unit in Lasem, Achmad Sholeh Syarifudin, apologised and took "full responsibility for the recovery of students and teachers".

He said the unit would conduct a comprehensive evaluation of its operation following the incident.

The head of Indonesia's National Nutrition Agency has said: "If it is identified that there was negligence and there are criminal elements, I apologise, we cannot help."

articles.title: 20 million children a year face online sexual abuse, UNICEF says
articles.summary: More than one in five children aged 12 to 17 were targeted on digital platforms, the UN children’s agency reports.
articles.body:
As many as 20 million children in 21 countries have experienced online sexual abuse or exploitation each year, according to new findings from the United Nations children’s agency, UNICEF.

More than one in five children aged 12 to 17 in countries in Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Eastern Europe have been targeted on digital platforms, according to the UNICEF report released on Thursday.

Researchers surveyed 21,000 children aged 12 to 17 who used the internet across 21 countries between 2020 and 2021, and then again between 2024 and 2025. They also conducted in-depth interviews with 100 young people who have experienced childhood abuse.

Social media facilitated more than half of the abuse cases, according to UNICEF, which cautioned that figures could be inaccurate due to underreporting by children. Less than 1 per cent of all abusive incidents were reported to authorities, the researchers found.

Last week, US social media giant Meta agreed to a landmark $18bn settlement in a major US federal case accusing the company of endangering children. Meta has faced an avalanche of legal cases this year, most arguing that it has deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive and that they have harmed children. The company has now agreed to make major changes to the features of its social media platforms.

What are the key findings of the UNICEF report?

The report estimated that in the periods studied, more than 15 million children were exposed to unwanted sexual content, nine million were asked to engage in sexual conversations or share sexual images against their will, and four million children had sexual images of themselves shared without their consent.

UNICEF said the issue is compounded by the fact that children often don’t recognise abuse or know who to report it to, and fear repercussions if they do. Formal systems can feel distant, complex or intimidating, the report noted.

“The report reveals a painful reality. More than 20 million children across the countries studied were subjected to unwanted explicit sexual content or exploitation online, often in the digital spaces where they learn, play, and connect with friends,” said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. “These experiences cause profound emotional and mental distress. Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help. We cannot look away.”

Information for the report was based on nationally representative survey data collected between 2020 and 2025 from approximately 21,000 internet-using children from the following countries:

Eastern and South Africa: Ethiopia, Kenya, Mozambique, Namibia, Tanzania and Uganda

Southeast Asia: Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam

Latin America and the Caribbean: Brazil, Colombia, the Dominican Republic and Mexico

Eastern Europe: Armenia, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia

Abuse often begins in public spaces, such as in schools or local neighbourhoods, before moving to digital spaces which can further facilitate harm.

Social media and messaging platforms enable different stages of abuse, “including initial contact, relationship-building, sexual solicitation, image-sharing, coercion, blackmail and the continued circulation of sexual content”, the report said.

Sometimes abuse takes place solely online.

According to the report’s findings, more than 60 percent of cases occurred on social media platforms, with the majority on Facebook (50 percent), WhatsApp (29 percent), Instagram (24 percent), SnapChat (13 percent) and TikTok (12 percent).

Most children do not seek help if they are being abused. Less than one percent of cases are reported to the police, a social worker or a helpline, while more than four in 10 cases not being disclosed to anyone at all.

“Children are not failing to report; they have correctly worked out that there is nowhere to report to,” Nighat Dad, executive director of the Pakistan-based Digital Rights Foundation, told Al Jazeera.

Dad, whose NGO works to provide safe online spaces in Pakistan, noted that incidents repeatedly occur online because of a “design problem – the message request, the move to a private chat, the reshare, the ability to return after being blocked”.

Many children minimise their experiences or do not recognise when they’ve been abused, she said.

Even when children do speak out, to a close friend, sibling, or parent, doing so may not necessarily stop the abuse or bring perpetrators to account.

UNICEF emphasised that its research interviews were the first time many of the children it interviewed had spoken to someone about the abuse they were subjected to.

Dad also cautioned that Pakistan, for example, is a “low-disclosure country” where notions of family “honour” and other cultural barriers prevent children from disclosing the harm they’ve experienced.

“A girl who speaks risks her phone, her schooling and sometimes her safety, and a boy is expected to cope in silence,” Dad said.

How does gender factor into online abuse?

Perpetrators often play on gender norms when exploiting children. Stigma and blame are used against girls to keep them silent, while boys are expected to cope alone, or threatened by perpetrators.

“Peer cultures and harmful norms around gender or masculinity can further normalise behaviours that cause significant harm, making abuse harder to recognise and address,” UNICEF noted.

What kind of impact does online sexual abuse have on children?

The repercussions are severe, UNICEF said: Children exposed to technology-facilitated sexual abuse and exploitation are four times more likely to have suicidal thoughts and to self-harm, along with higher levels of anxiety.

In Mexico or North Macedonia, for example, the risk of suicidal thoughts or behaviours was more than eight times higher among children who experienced abuse, while in Pakistan the risk of self-harm was more than seven times higher than average, the report found.

Abuse extends well beyond the digital sphere, seeping into children’s everyday lives, schooling and relationships.

UNICEF said the onus to protect children online must be placed on governments and technology companies, which must change how online spaces are designed and regulated.

It also highlighted that while children often take steps to protect each other, societies, schools and families must work to shift the burden of protection away from children.

Citing Meta’s recent settlement, Dad acknowledged that design changes, such as better age verification and parental controls, can and should happen.

“For years those of us working outside the US were told these defaults would break the product. Meta has now shown the product can change.”

A spokesperson for Meta told Al Jazeera, “This report is based on surveys from as far back as 2020, before we introduced the protections UNICEF recommends, like automatically defaulting teens into private accounts and preventing adults from messaging teens they’re not connected to.

“While the report doesn’t provide any specific evidence of abuse, we’ll continue to fight child exploitation aggressively across our apps and support law enforcement in prosecuting the criminals behind it.”

The spokesperson also pointed out that Meta-owned WhatsApp is a private messaging service rather than a social media platform. “We don’t have algorithms that make a piece of content more or less likely to be viewed, and you need someone’s phone number or exact username to connect with them for the first time.”

Snapchat and TikTok have not responded to requests for comment for Al Jazeera.

articles.body: A 911 call made moments after a 5-year-old autistic girl disappeared from a South Carolina rental home captures her father reporting her missing and saying he needed to check the nearby water. A massive search ended Monday after authorities found Saylor Hayes’ body in waters near Pawleys Island, South Carolina. Her parents were arrested in Tennessee the following day. articles.title: Houthi fighters clash with Yemeni government forces in country’s southwest
articles.summary: Houthis attempt to cut road linking Taiz to al-Makha in apparent bid to sever government’s strategic supply route.
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces are engaged in fierce clashes with Houthi fighters across several fronts west of Taiz province, as the Iran-backed group launches a broad offensive along front lines on the western Red Sea coast.

In the latest sign that a return to full-scale war in Yemen may be approaching, Houthi fighters on Thursday attempted to advance to reach and cut the road linking Taiz to al-Makha (Mocha), aiming to sever Taiz city from the coast.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Yemeni capital Sanaa, said taking control of the port city of al-Makha would cut off government forces from a strategic supply route and give Houthis a foothold in the Red Sea, a key maritime route for oil exports and other global trade.

“In order to do that, they must drive out Yemeni government forces,” Mawry said. “But we have reports from Yemeni government officials that they have regained control of some of the areas that fell under Houthi control.”

Yemen’s Army Media Centre said Houthis had fired 14 ballistic missiles and launched drones at populated districts in the provinces of Taiz and Hodeidah.

It said the Houthis launched an attack on army positions in the Maqbanah Mountains, west of Taiz province, and attempted to infiltrate areas of al-Ahtoub, al-Tuwair, al-Kadha and Jabal Ghabari.

The media centre said more than 18 Houthi fighters were killed and others wounded or captured as they clashed with Yemeni forces in the southwestern part of the country on Thursday.

An unnamed military source, meanwhile, told the AFP news agency that 13 government forces were killed in the fighting. Another military source said most of those killed were on the front lines between al-Makha and Taiz, while the others died in clashes near the Red Sea coast.

A field officer in al-Makha told AFP his men were “fighting fiercely to repel the massive Houthi offensive”.

“We also thwarted an attack with two booby-trapped boats that exploded near the port,” he said, requesting anonymity.

The Yemen News Agency, Saba, reported that the army shot down three Houthi drones in the Jabal Habashi district in Taiz governorate and was engaged in fierce clashes with Houthi fighters on the al-Barah front, west of Taiz city.

Over the past weeks, fighting has intensified in Yemen, with exchanges of fire and drone attacks reported across nearly the entire frozen front line.

Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year that spiralled into a years-long war.

The Houthis and the internationally recognised government struck a truce in 2022 that has, until now, largely held. Progress towards a lasting agreement to end the war stalled in 2023, when Israel launched its war on Gaza and tensions in the wider region escalated.

Al Jazeera’s Mawry said the fact that Houthi fighters were able to enter government territory and seize it for several hours was a sign that attempts at resuming talks and establishing a ceasefire were failing.

“Both sides are now scrabbling to gain territory and gain control not just on land, but at sea,” the correspondent said. In recent weeks, Houthis have launched attacks on government-affiliated Saudi oil tankers .

“We’ll have to wait and see whether government forces can maintain control”, Mawry added, noting that the army must work to thwart the Houthis’ “fierce advancement”.

articles.title: Nepal floods: No bodies to cremate, kin burn kusha effigies as hopes fade for  missing
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT): Families in flood-ravaged Nuwakot and Rasuwa who could not find missing relatives — or their bodies — began performing symb.
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT): Families in flood-ravaged Nuwakot and Rasuwa who could not find missing relatives — or their bodies — began performing symbolic cremations with human-shaped effigies made from kusha, a sacred grass used in Hindu rituals.After days of searching hospitals, morgues, riverbanks and recovery lists, relatives lit the effigies on pyres at cremation sites so they could begin mourning.In Nuwakot, families gathered along Trishuli river for the rites as priests shaped bundles of kusha to represent the missing person, placed them on wooden pyres and guided relatives through the same rituals normally performed over a body.Families from Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit districts, also began holding such funerals or travelling to cremation grounds after repeated searches failed to locate their kin.Rozel Shrestha, 12, performed the rites for his father, Krishna Shrestha, 37, who disappeared in Rasuwa.Krishna’s brother Jeevan Shrestha said the family had searched widely before accepting that they might never recover his body.“We searched everywhere, went to morgues across the country, but could not find his body,” he said. “The family eventually decided we had to perform our traditional rituals to liberate his soul.”Relatives of Raj Kumar Shrestha, 30, performed his last rites with a kusha effigy after searching for six days. The family had received a photograph of a body resembling him and travelled to Simtar in Nuwakot, but the body had already been moved.They could not trace it afterwards. Nirajan Poudel of Bidur municipality performed rites for five relatives — his parents, uncle, aunt and cousin — after none could be found.Similar scenes later unfolded at Pashupati Aryaghat in Kathmandu, where more than 100 kusha effigies were cremated in a single day. Tapindra Prasad Timalsina was among those who performed last rites there for Sabin, 21. A priest prepared the effigy and relatives poured water over it before Timalsina lit the pyre. “It weighs heavily on my heart,” he said.Devmani Bhattarai, a professor at Nepal Sanskrit University, said Hindu scriptures permit families to perform last rites with an effigy when a body cannot be recovered and there is clear evidence that a relative was swept away or if an entire settlement was destroyed. “If the body has not been found, there is no time to wait,” he told TOI on phone.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: British trekker found dead in Pakistan after disappearing during mountain descent
articles.summary: UK News: Alexander Harris, a 30-year-old British trekker, was found dead after going missing during a descent from Musa Ka Musala in northern Pakistan. His body was discovered by search teams after he separated from his hiking companion.
articles.body: A British trekker has been found dead after disappearing during a descent from a mountain in northern Pakistan.Alexander Harris, 30, from Birmingham, had been descending Musa Ka Musala in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Saturday when he became separated from his hiking companion. His body was later found on a forest path, BBC reported.Khalid Iqbal, the area's deputy commissioner, said police and volunteers had spent hours searching for Harris before locating him.“He most probably slipped and fell,” Iqbal said.Harris had started the trek at about 5.40 am local time with another hiker. The pair reached the summit, which stands at just over 4,000 metres (13,000ft), and took photographs before beginning their descent.They became separated after Harris moved ahead of his companion by about 1-2km. Rain then began to fall in the area.“There was a difference in their speed,” Iqbal said. “He was moving faster, he got about 1- 2 km ahead. Then it started raining.”Around 250 to 300 people, including police officers and volunteers, were involved in the search, according to Iqbal. Teams searched the mountainous terrain on foot and used drones, although poor visibility restricted aerial operations.Harris had been living in Islamabad, where he worked for global advisory firm Adam Smith International. He also held Irish citizenship.Officials said Harris and his companion had not informed authorities about their planned trek. Iqbal said the hotel where Harris was staying had offered him a guide and police security, but he declined the assistance.“He said that he knew the area and did not need any help,” Iqbal said.The search teams worked through heavy rain, fog and poor visibility across steep terrain before finding Harris.The Foreign Office said it was supporting Harris's family and was in contact with local authorities in Pakistan.Harris was a keen hiker and trail runner, regularly taking part in long-distance races in Pakistan. His running group, Margalla Trail Runners, described him as a “passionate trail runner” in a social media tribute.“May his soul rest in peace and may his family and loved ones find strength and comfort during this difficult time,” the group said.The Foreign Office said: “Our thoughts are with Alex's family, friends and colleagues at this incredibly difficult time. We remain focused on supporting his family.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Israeli medics train US synagogues how to respond to attacks, as high holidays approach
articles.summary: Magen David Adom and Community Security Service train synagogue volunteers in mass casualty response as antisemitism fears grow before Rosh Hashanah.
articles.body: Jewish communities across the U.S. are ramping up their security measures and emergency preparation ahead of Rosh Hashanah and other High Holidays. Israel's emergency medical service, Magen David Adom, partnered with the U.S.-based Community Security Service to hold trainings for security volunteers at synagogues across the country. Senior paramedic Aryeh Myers told Fox News Digital that community members remain deeply concerned about a rise in antisemitism. "There is this heightened sense of concern, of worry that these attacks are now a question of when rather than if," Myers said in an interview. MARYLAND SYNAGOGUE SUES COUNTY OVER LAW RESTRICTING CONCEALED CARRY NEAR HOUSES OF WORSHIP Myers has held First 7 Minutes trainings in the U.S. and elsewhere with Jewish, Christian and non-religious groups, teaching volunteers how to respond in the minutes after an attack has occurred and before first responders have arrived. His trainings focus on first aid, how to communicate most effectively with first responders and how best to assist them once they do arrive. MAN CHARGED WITH ASSAULT, HATE CRIMES AFTER ALLEGEDLY DISRUPTING SHABBAT SERVICES AT NYC SYNAGOGUE "Our expertise is in response to mass casualty events.... We respond on the national level to everything from delivering babies, to terror attacks to war situations," Myers said. "The advantage that Magen David Adom brings is unfortunately having that level of experience, that we have seen multiple mass casualty attacks and multi-casualty attacks and have learned from those," he added. ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE ESCALATES AS DEADLY WEAPON ATTACKS SURGE IN 2025: REPORT Jewish communities across the globe have faced increasing levels of antisemitism in the years since the October 7 terror attacks in Israel. Many U.S. universities became hotbeds for anti-Israel and antisemitic attacks amid Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza. JEWISH EDUCATORS FACE RAMPANT ANTISEMITISM IN TEACHERS UNIONS, NEW REPORT FINDS A new report from the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) found that Jewish teachers have also faced rampant antisemitism from teachers unions. The organization surveyed 307 Jewish members of teachers unions, many of whom admitted to censoring themselves and being disappointed with how unions handled concerns about antisemitism. BACK TO SCHOOL SHOULD NOT MEAN BACK TO FEAR FOR JEWISH STUDENTS "What we found is not the work of a few bad actors. It is a structural and cultural failure," ADL CEO Jonathan Greenblatt said in a statement. "Jewish educators deserve to feel safe and protected in their union spaces. And instead of that, they are self-censoring and fearing backlash for raising concerns." Sydney Altfield, CEO of Teach Coalition, an organization that advocates for Jewish schools, said the report was particularly concerning because teachers unions were meant to represent and protect all educators. THE BRAVEST JEWS IN AMERICA ARE 15 YEARS OLD — AND THEY’RE GOING BACK TO SCHOOL "What strikes me is that these unions are supposed to be homes for everyone, and [they're] not being that," Altfield told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP One of the key findings of the report was the high rate at which Jewish educators were self-censoring out of fear of retaliation. According to the ADL, 70% of respondents "somewhat or strongly agreed" that bringing up concerns about how Jews were treated in union spaces "could lead to reputational or professional consequences." Fox News' Rachel Wolf contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump calls media ‘treasonous scum’ over reports of low Iran war munitions
articles.summary: Comments latest swipe by president against critical media coverage of what experts call troubling shortages.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has again pushed back on media reports detailing dangerously low munitions stockpiles as the US-Israel war with Iran stretches into its seventh month.

In a post on his Truth Social account, Trump said the military was producing munitions at “levels never seen before” and has “far more than we could ever use”.

He also again took aim at media outlets that have reported on US shortages of both offensive and defensive weapons, calling them “treasonous scum” who refuse to “accurately report” on the war with Iran.

Trump made similar comments about news reports of munitions shortages in August, after the Washington Post reported he had grown frustrated with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the supply shortages.

At the time, Trump said those reports were “treasonous statements” and promised whoever had leaked the information to the press would be “hunted down” and that “long term jail sentences will be sought”.

Numerous US news outlets have reported on the toll the Iran war has had on US military munitions and other supplies, especially those needed for protecting US bases and regional allies against Iran-launched missiles and drones.

The reports have been backed by experts, including the Washington, DC-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), which said in July that the US had just more than a third of its Patriot missile interceptors left, and about half its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors.

Large portions of offensive weapons stockpiles, including Tomahawk missiles, Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles (JASSMs) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSMs), have also been used in the war, according to CSIS.

Even with a slate of new Trump administration agreements with defence contractors meant to accelerate production, experts have warned that replenishing US supplies of key weapons could take at least two years.

In the short term, the shortages could harm deterrence against adversaries with more advanced weapons technology than Iran, former military officials have warned .

Press freedom groups, meanwhile, have said Trump has taken a number of alarming steps against critical media outlets since returning to office in 2025.

Trump has asked federal broadcast regulators to pull licences for media outlets in response to their coverage.

Federal prosecutors have also taken the unusual step of subpoenaing an increasing number of journalists in an effort to track down confidential sources in the administration who have leaked information to the press.

articles.title: ‘Never seen destruction like this’: Even seasoned relief workers shaken by scale of Nepal disaster
articles.summary: South Asia News: DEHRADUN: Several Indian and Nepalese NGOs are working on the ground to provide survivors with hot meals, medical care and other essential supplies. T.
articles.body: DEHRADUN: Several Indian and Nepalese NGOs are working on the ground to provide survivors with hot meals, medical care and other essential supplies. Those involved in relief operations, including veterans of many disasters, say that the “scale of devastation they are witnessing this time has shaken many of them”.Harteerath Singh of Gurgaon-based Hemkunt Foundation, who is currently in Rasuwa, said his organisation has worked in disasters across the globe since 2010, including the 2015 Nepal earthquake, Taal volcano eruption in the Philippines, Covid-19 pandemic and the recent floods in Punjab and Assam.“I’ve never seen such destruction in my life. The loss of life and property here is unparalleled. There have been instances here in Nepal where we reached an affected area with aid material but found nobody to hand it over,” Singh told TOI from Nepal on Thursday.He further informed that he along with 21 other volunteers of the organisation has been carrying out relief work in Rasuwa, Dhading and Nuwakot, which have been the worst-affected areas.“We are focusing on running community kitchens to provide fresh meals to the survivors, dry ration and medicines. We’ve also made bedding sets comprising a mattress, pillow, mosquito net and bed-sheet, which will be airdropped from helicopters in the affected areas that are inaccessible by road,” said Singh, adding that connectivity issues are hampering their effort.He also claimed that he and other volunteers are carrying out the task of cleaning of recovered bodies for the rituals before cremation. “We are dedicated to doing sewa...”Kanchan Jha of Nepal-based NGO Sano Paila (Little Step) echoed similar sentiments. His organisation has worked in the aftermath of the civil war, the 2015 earthquake, floods in Madhesh province and the Covid-19 pandemic.“Bhotekoshi flood was markedly different from previous disasters, particularly the 2015 earthquake, because of its impact on survivors’ mental state. In the 2015 quake, people had confidence in finding their loved ones and rising up again. This time, the survivors seem to have no hope. They don’t know where to go to seek help or where to find their missing ones,” Jha said.He also claimed that another major difference this time is the lack of presence of local administration in the affected areas unlike during the earthquake.“Because, the local administration officials are themselves the survivors now. Such was the destruction caused by the floods,” said Jha who added that a team of around eight volunteers of his NGO, are running community kitchens in Rasuwa to provide much-needed hot meals to the survivors.Saurav Rimal of another Nepal-based NGO, Karmayog Foundation, meanwhile flagged risk of spreading of airborne diseases among the survivors due the stench of decomposing bodies in the affected areas.“Not just survivors, but social workers, too, are at risk of getting seriously ill due to the stench of dead bodies. Also, witnessing the suffering and sorrow of survivors is taking a toll on our mental state. There are orphaned children, crying in front of us, which breaks our hearts. We are determined not to leave them and other survivors alone despite several challenges in the relief works,” said Rimal.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: FOX News Media announces extensive 9/11 anniversary coverage from Ground Zero, Pentagon and Shanksville
articles.summary: FOX News Media announces extensive 9/11 anniversary coverage with live broadcasts from Ground Zero, Washington, D.C., and Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
articles.body: FOX News Media will honor the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on America with extensive multiplatform special programming, the company announced on Thursday. On the somber anniversary, and in the days leading up to it, Fox News personalities and correspondents will present commemorative packages and interviews while reporting live from locations across New York, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania. "FOX & Friends" will spend the week of Sept. 7 broadcasting live from several locations tied to the horrific day. Co-host Steve Doocy, who was broadcasting live alongside co-host Brian Kilmeade on the morning of the attacks in 2001, will host the program’s flagship "Breakfast with Friends" series live from the historic O’Hara’s Pub in New York City just two blocks from Ground Zero. MASSIVE PIECE OF 9/11 HISTORY MAKES STUNNING 10,500-MILE JOURNEY ACROSS AMERICA Doocy will then travel to Washington, D.C., on Tuesday and speak with Tunnel to Towers Foundation chairman and CEO Frank Siller. The show will also feature the Steel Across America tour — a historic coast-to-coast campaign honoring those who sacrificed their lives on 9/11 — arriving at the White House. Doocy will broadcast live from Shanksville, Pennsylvania, the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93, on Thursday. On Friday, Fox News Channel’s special coverage will commence with "FOX & Friends" co-hosts Kilmeade, Ainsley Earhardt and Lawrence Jones broadcasting live from the Hyatt House in Jersey City, overlooking the New York City skyline. Doocy will contribute live from Ground Zero. "America’s Newsroom" co-anchors Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino will broadcast live from Brookfield Place overlooking the World Trade Center campus in downtown Manhattan. The reading of the victims’ names from the National September 11 Memorial & Museum is also expected to air during "America’s Newsroom." TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE "The Faulkner Focus," "Outnumbered," "America Reports" and "The Will Cain Show" will all feature special segments and interviews tied to 9/11, while Martha MacCallum’s "The Story" will report live from the Hyatt House and feature interviews with Cardinal Timothy Dolan and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch. Throughout the day, Fox News senior correspondent Eric Shawn, who reported from Ground Zero on the day of the attacks, will contribute live from downtown Manhattan and correspondent Alexis McAdams will report live from Shanksville. Chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin will contribute from the Pentagon and senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy will be stationed at the White House. On Fox Business Network, "The Claman Countdown" anchor Liz Claman will commemorate the 658 Cantor Fitzgerald employees lost in the 9/11 attacks on Sept. 10. The following day, Claman will feature an interview with Silverstein Properties CEO Larry Silverstein from the World Trade Center, which he helped rebuild following the attacks. AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS Fox News Digital will publish multiple retrospective and feature stories focused on survivors, first responders, victims’ families and those carrying the legacy of 9/11 forward 25 years later. Fox News Digital will also provide day-of coverage of the commemorations at Ground Zero, the Pentagon and Shanksville, including livestream embeds from all three ceremonies. Fox News Digital will also feature interviews with National September 11 Memorial & Museum CEO Elizabeth L. Hillman and former Navy SEAL Robert O’Neill, among others. The platform will publish a "Never Forget" archival photo retrospective, including a look at how Ground Zero and the Manhattan skyline have changed since the attacks. FOX Nation will debut two new specials ahead of the anniversary, starting with "Paul Mauro’s Notes from Ground Zero" on Sept. 4. The special spotlights Fox News contributor and former NYPD Inspector Paul Mauro, who was working the morning of 9/11 and scribbled down notes in the days following the attacks, as he returns to Ground Zero for the first time in 25 years. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE On September 8, FOX Nation will launch "Born on 9/11: 25 Years with Harris Faulkner," exploring the lives of people born on September 11, 2001. FOX Nation will also livestream the official ceremonies at the NYC memorial site and the Pentagon next Friday. FOX News Audio and FOX News Podcasts will present extensive coverage of the anniversary as well, including an eight-part documentary series entitled "FOX News Rewind: 9/11," that features a variety of Fox News personalities. On YouTube, "The Brian Kilmeade Show" will provide access to some of Kilmeade’s most notable 9/11 interviews and affiliates will be offered an anniversary special from Kilmeade that reflects on how America has evolved over the last 25 years.
